feedback: If the lamp does not light, check that the bridge actually touches both contacts and that the rest of the loop is complete — a break anywhere stops it.
If a learner thinks only 'one side' needs connecting, show that current must travel all the way round the whole loop; a single contact is not enough.
activities.intendedInsight: Closing a switch is nothing more than bridging a gap with a conductor to complete the loop; a switch is a deliberate, controllable version of the 'break in the loop' from earlier circuit work.
learnerActions: Make a switch from two drawing pins and a paperclip, or two foil tabs, placed in a simple series circuit with a cell and a lamp (or buzzer).
Bridge the two contacts with the paperclip (or foil) and observe the lamp light; lift the bridge to break the gap and watch it go out.
Describe in your own words that closing the switch simply bridges a gap with a conductor, completing the loop.
activities.title: Build your own switch from everyday materials

feedback: For a wrong match, return to a worked or operated example and re-trace the loop: open = gap = broken = off.
If a learner says electricity waits or piles up at the open switch, trace the broken loop together — an open gap means no current flows anywhere, so nothing accumulates.
Treat this as a check of the mapping, not where the intuition is first built — pair it with hands-on operation.
activities.intendedInsight: Confirms the learner can read a switch's state and predict the lamp result, reinforces the correct vocabulary, and checks that an open loop means no flow anywhere rather than electricity stored at the switch.
learnerActions: Match OPEN to off and CLOSED to on, and look at circuit images with the switch in each state to decide whether the lamp lights.
Answer 'which switch position lights the lamp?' and justify why.
When off, consider where the electricity is: trace the broken loop to see that flow stops everywhere and nothing piles up at the switch.
activities.title: Check the open↔off, closed↔on mapping
